title: Research Explained #18 -- Can Two Observers Disagree About Whether a Signal Traveled Faster Than Light?
html:
Beyond the Light Barrier — Research Explained #18

Reference Frames, Relativity, and the Problem of Causality

Imagine a message sent between two distant stations. One observer assigns transmission a time earlier than reception. A second observer, moving relative to the first, assigns reception an earlier time than transmission. Can both descriptions be correct?

For two spacelike separated events, special relativity says yes. But the title needs a careful answer: inertial observers cannot disagree about whether the separation is spacelike, lightlike, or timelike. They can disagree about the time order of spacelike events. If a hypothetical signal directly connects spacelike separated events in flat spacetime, every inertial frame classifies that connection as superluminal, although its coordinate speed and time direction can differ.

That distinction takes us from clock synchronization to one of the hardest questions for any proposed faster-than-light communication or travel system: can its allowed operations form a closed chain of influence?

1. What an observer and a reference frame mean

An event is a particular occurrence at a place and time: pressing a transmit button, or recording a message at a receiver. A reference frame assigns coordinates to events. An inertial frame is one in which freely moving test bodies follow straight paths at constant velocity when gravity is negligible. Here we use ideal flat spacetime, one spatial dimension, and standard Einstein synchronization.

In these calculations, an “observer” means a frame equipped with a network of stationary, synchronized clocks and position markers. It does not mean merely what one person sees through a telescope. Light takes time to reach an eye; we must account for that delay before comparing event coordinates.

Proper time is what a clock measures along its own path, or worldline. Coordinate time labels events throughout a chosen frame. Comparing distant clocks requires a synchronization procedure; reading one local clock does not.

Einstein synchronization uses a light signal sent from one clock, reflected at a distant clock, and received back. The reflection is assigned the midpoint between sending and return times. The resulting synchronized clocks belong to that frame. A moving frame uses its own synchronization and generally disagrees about which distant events are simultaneous. Einstein's original paper develops this operational starting point and the Lorentz transformation. [1, §§1–3]

2. Why “at the same time” depends on motion

Let frame S′ move at velocity v along the positive x direction of frame S. Their origins coincide when both coordinate times are zero. For differences between two events, the Lorentz transformation is:

Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c2)

Δx′ = γ(Δx − vΔt)

γ = 1/√(1 − v2/c2),   |v| < c.

Here Δ means “second event minus first event”; t is time in seconds, x is position in metres, v is frame velocity in metres per second, and c is the vacuum speed of light. A prime identifies the moving frame. The Lorentz factor γ is dimensionless. The term vΔx/c² has units of seconds, so the time equation is dimensionally consistent.

If two distant events are simultaneous in S, then Δt = 0, but:

Δt′ = −γvΔx/c2.

Except when the relevant velocity or separation vanishes, those events are not simultaneous in S′. This is the relativity of simultaneity. It is a difference in how frames assign time across space, not a faulty clock or an uncorrected visual delay. [1]

In engineering terms, each frame has a consistent distributed clock system. Relative motion changes how the two systems assign timestamps to distant events. Neither system is the universal master clock assumed by everyday intuition.

3. What all inertial frames agree about

Use the sign convention:

Δs2 = c2Δt2 − Δx2.

In three spatial dimensions, also subtract Δy² and Δz². Substituting the Lorentz transformation gives c²Δt′² − Δx′² = c²Δt² − Δx². This invariant sorts distinct events into three classes:

  • Timelike: Δs² > 0. A slower-than-light traveler can connect them. All ordinary inertial frames that preserve the future direction agree on their order.
  • Lightlike, or null: Δs² = 0. A vacuum light ray can connect them in flat spacetime. Such frames again agree on their order.
  • Spacelike: Δs² < 0. The separation exceeds the distance light could travel during the time between them. Some inertial frames reverse their time order.

A light cone marks the possible directions of light propagation from an event. Ordinary material trajectories remain inside the cone; vacuum light lies on it. Spacelike events lie outside it. A mathematical spacelike connection is not evidence that a controllable signal can traverse it.

For spacelike events with a finite nonzero Δt′, the invariant inequality gives |Δx′/Δt′| > c. A frame with Δt′ = 0 instead assigns zero elapsed coordinate time; the corresponding speed ratio is undefined, often informally called infinite. No boost turns that separation into an ordinary slower-than-light connection. These statements are direct algebraic consequences of the transformation, not a proposed FTL mechanism.

4. A numerical example you can check

Classification: Category 6 — analytic calculation, conditional on an invented FTL connection. This is a teaching example, not a BTLB simulation or measurement.

In frame S, let hypothetical transmission event A occur at t = 0, x = 0. Let reception event B occur at t = 1 second, x = 2 light-seconds. One light-second is the distance vacuum light travels in one second: c × 1 s. Thus the assigned speed is u = Δx/Δt = 2c.

Choose v = 0.8c. Then γ = 1/√(1 − 0.8²) = 5/3. Applying the transformation:

Δt′ = (5/3)[1 s − (0.8c)(2c·s)/c²] = −1 s.

Δx′ = (5/3)[2c·s − (0.8c)(1 s)] = 2c·s.

Δs² = (1 − 4)c²s² = −3c²s².

Δs′² = (1 − 4)c²s² = −3c²s².

Same two hypothetical events, different coordinates
Quantity, B minus A Frame S Frame S′
Time difference +1 s −1 s
Position difference +2 light-seconds +2 light-seconds
Signed coordinate velocity +2c −2c
Separation type Spacelike Spacelike

Frame S′ assigns B a timestamp one second earlier than A. The minus sign in its velocity ratio comes from the negative time difference; it does not mean changing a frame has created a second message. A and B still label the same physical interactions if such interactions can occur. Whether a consistent FTL theory permits them with those operational roles is an additional dynamical question.

For a general hypothetical forward connection with Δx = uΔt, u > c, and Δt > 0:

Δt′ = γΔt(1 − vu/c2).

Its time order reverses when v > c²/u. Because u > c, this threshold can lie below c. In our example the threshold is 0.5c, so 0.8c reverses the order.

Two checks help catch mistakes: at v = 0 the original coordinates return; at v = 0.5c the events are simultaneous in S′. For a forward vacuum light ray, u = c gives Δt′ = γΔt(1 − v/c) > 0 for |v| < c, so its order cannot reverse.

5. Reversing two timestamps is not yet a causal loop

One spacelike link and two coordinate descriptions do not by themselves form a loop. There is no return route in that example. To demonstrate a closed chain of influence, one must specify additional allowed paths and show how information returns to an earlier event on the original sender's own worldline.

That last condition is stronger than a negative distant time difference. If Alice receives a reply before she sends the original message, both events occur at Alice's location. Their order is the order recorded by her own clock. It cannot be removed by changing inertial frames.

A tachyonic antitelephone is a hypothetical signaling arrangement that attempts exactly this. Here “tachyonic” means an assumed superluminal signaling capability; no tachyon transmitter is being claimed. The classic literature examines causal contradictions under such assumptions. [2]

6. The antitelephone depends on specific assumptions

For the simple construction below, assume all of the following:

  1. Flat spacetime and the usual Lorentz transformation apply to the stations and their clocks.
  2. Alice and Bob move inertially relative to each other, and can exchange controllable information over hypothetical superluminal links.
  3. Each sender can emit toward the other at speed magnitude u > c, forward in that sender's own rest-frame time. This availability in both moving frames is an extra physical assumption; it is not supplied by the coordinate transformation.
  4. The required directions, reception, and conditional retransmission are possible. In this idealized example Bob replies immediately; real processing delays would have to be included.
  5. No preferred time ordering or other dynamical restriction forbids one of the two links.

A two-way information channel is crucial. A pattern speed, a correlation with no selectable message, or a geometric line on a plot does not provide it. A theory that permits superluminal propagation only toward increasing time in a preferred frame would not automatically allow this construction. Such a restriction would itself need a specified physical theory and tests; naming it does not establish viability.

A complete conditional round trip

Classification: Category 6 — analytic consistency test of hypothetical operations. This is a separate example from Section 4. Measure positions in light-seconds and times in seconds, so c has numerical value 1 in the following equations. Let Alice remain at x = 0. Bob passes her at t = 0 and moves along x = 0.8t. The primed frame is Bob's rest frame; its origin coincides with Alice's at their meeting.

Alice waits until event P at (t, x) = (1, 0), then sends at u = 4c in her frame. The outgoing path is x = 4(t − 1). It meets Bob where:

4(t − 1) = 0.8t,   giving Q: (t, x) = (5/4, 1).

Transform Q with γ = 5/3:

t′Q = (5/3)(5/4 − 0.8 × 1) = 3/4;   x′Q = 0.

Bob immediately sends a reply toward Alice at −4c in his frame. Its path is x′ = −4(t′ − 3/4). Alice's worldline in that frame is x′ = −0.8t′. Their intersection satisfies:

−0.8t′ = −4(t′ − 3/4),   so t′R = 15/16,   x′R = −3/4.

On Alice's worldline t′ = γt, hence:

tR = (15/16)/(5/3) = 9/16 s = 0.5625 s.

Alice receives at R, 0.4375 seconds before her transmission at P. Bob's reply is forward in his own time: 15/16 − 3/4 = 3/16 second. Alice's original transmission is forward in her own time. Yet the combined allowed links return information to Alice's earlier proper time.

Adding the ordinary future-directed segment of Alice's worldline from R to P closes the chain R → P → Q → R. In this toy extension, the two superluminal legs are spacelike in the Minkowski metric; the chain is therefore not an ordinary general-relativistic closed timelike curve in that metric. It is a closed influence loop under the added FTL rules.

A self-defeating protocol—“send at P only if no reply arrived at R,” with Bob replying whenever he receives—exposes a contradiction if unrestricted conditional operations are assumed. This is a consistency problem for that set of assumptions, not experimental evidence of messages from the future. Restrictions, self-consistency proposals, or other modified dynamics require their own analysis; none follows merely from drawing reversed timestamps.

Finite delays can remove the loop for a particular setup. Conversely, a single unsuccessful arrangement does not prove every possible arrangement safe. The allowed speeds, relative motion, separation, response times, and channel rules must be analyzed together.

7. Why wormholes and warp metrics need global analysis

The flat-spacetime calculation cannot simply be pasted onto an arbitrary curved spacetime. In general relativity, light cones are defined locally by the spacetime metric. A traveler can remain locally slower than light along a timelike path, while a hypothetical geometry offers an earlier arrival than a specified route through an external region. This is different from a local spacelike signal in unchanged Minkowski spacetime.

For a proposed traversable wormhole, the complete geometry must specify how its two mouths connect, their motion, their clock relationship, and the external paths between them. A traversable spatial shortcut alone does not establish a time machine. A sufficiently large mouth time offset, combined with an available external return path, can create closed causal paths in certain models. Morris, Thorne, and Yurtsever analyzed this conditional possibility; their paper did not demonstrate a constructed wormhole. [3]

For a proposed warp geometry, local timelike motion does not settle the global question either. One must examine the full spacetime, including its exterior, transitions, and any allowed combinations of journeys. Alcubierre introduced a speculative metric with an effective superluminal travel interpretation; Everett subsequently exhibited a modified construction admitting causal loops. These are mathematical analyses, not propulsion demonstrations, and they do not mean every metric described as “warp” has the same causal structure. [4] [5]

A closed timelike curve is a path that remains future-directed and timelike locally yet returns to the same spacetime event. A closed causal curve can also include null segments. These are global geometric properties, independent of coordinate relabeling. A proposed FTL channel with additional propagation rules also needs analysis of the influence paths allowed by those rules, whether or not those paths are metric-causal.

One useful sufficient safeguard is a globally defined time function that strictly increases along every allowed future-directed path. If a path returned to its starting event, the same function would have to be both larger and unchanged, which is impossible. Finding a coordinate called t is insufficient: its monotonicity must be established across the relevant domain and all permitted paths. Failure to find such a function is not by itself proof of a loop.

Any causal conclusion must state its domain and boundary conditions. A finite grid or a single traced ray cannot prove that a loop is absent throughout a complete spacetime. Nor does absence of a loop prove that a metric has a realizable source, stable evolution, controllable horizons, or a feasible creation and shutdown process.

Hawking's chronology protection conjecture concerns whether physical laws prevent the formation of closed timelike curves. It should not be treated as a universal, experimentally established mechanism that automatically repairs every speculative geometry. [6]

8. What this requires of Beyond the Light Barrier

BTLB's Research Method v1.2 requires us to keep mathematical possibility, physical source feasibility, numerical behavior, and experimental evidence separate. The supplied Research State v1.11 says no project result establishes FTL communication, warp propulsion, or a physically realized traversable wormhole. It also records Category 8 independent scientific reproduction as NONE and Category 9 physical experimental evidence as NONE. These are statements about that supplied project record, not an assertion that this article has audited all later work. [I1–I2]

The existing WC-MGT-1 carrier calculations are Category 7 work on an assumed background geometry. Their internal cross-validation does not establish a physical channel or global causal consistency. The retained low-frequency electromagnetic scan found no useful transmission resonance in its scanned configuration; that null result is not erased by discussing more attractive possibilities. Source realizability remains unresolved. [I2, §4]

The Shared Field Map proposes a shared null-ray and moving-endpoint benchmark suite on known spacetimes before speculative geometries. The Verification Roadmap includes causality among the WD physics gates. This article recommends adding the following explicit checks to any relevant future candidate assessment; it does not claim those checks have already been implemented or passed. [I3–I4]

  1. Define the information-transfer claim. Specify controllable input, received output, endpoints, clock procedure, and the light-travel comparison. Separate a local speed claim from a global shortcut claim.
  2. Recover established limits. Verify Minkowski light cones, Lorentz transformations, timelike and null order preservation, and the analytic examples here before interpreting speculative outputs.
  3. Specify the complete model. Record metric and version, topology and mouth identifications if applicable, source assumptions, time orientation, exterior, initial and boundary conditions, and allowed operations.
  4. Test return paths and composition. Include moving endpoints, multiple uses, channel direction restrictions, processing delays, and formation/shutdown. Search for a return to the sender's earlier proper time rather than relying on a negative coordinate timestamp.
  5. Record the scope of every outcome. Preserve counterexamples, null results, unresolved regions, numerical resolution and convergence limits. A search finding no loop is bounded computational evidence, not a global proof.

The same causal responsibility applies if information is carried on a physical storage device by a hypothetical FTL-capable vehicle. The roadmap distinguishes such propulsion-mediated courier transport from a direct WC channel, but an operationally superluminal information route still needs causal analysis. [I4, V5 communication/data-return gate]

9. Evidence classification for this article

Research Method v1.2 categories and the limits of the present article
Category Application here
1 — Established experimental/observational evidence The article relies on the empirically supported framework of relativity; it reports no new measurement and provides no evidence of FTL signals.
2 — Accepted physical theory Lorentz transformations, invariant interval classification, and local/global causal distinctions within their stated theoretical domains.
3 — Published speculative theory Tachyonic signaling scenarios and the cited traversable-wormhole and warp constructions; publication does not establish physical realization.
4 — BTLB project hypothesis No new BTLB FTL mechanism is introduced or validated.
5 — Engineering concept Hypothetical stations and communication protocols illustrate assumptions; they are not apparatus specifications.
6 — Analytic estimate/calculation The two worked numerical examples, interval checks, and order-reversal threshold.
7 — Numerical or simulation result No new simulation is reported. Existing WC results are mentioned only with their supplied-record qualifications.
8 — Independently reproduced result Not claimed. Arithmetic checks within this preparation are not independent scientific reproduction.
9 — Experimental result None reported. No physical FTL, wormhole, warp, or causal-loop demonstration is claimed.

10. What the question really asks us to establish

Two inertial observers can disagree about the order of spacelike separated events. They agree on the spacelike classification. A reversal of distant coordinate timestamps alone is not a closed causal loop.

The serious consistency test begins when a proposed physical mechanism supplies controllable connections, return routes, and operational rules. Some hypothetical sets of rules produce a reply before the sender's own transmission; others restrict the necessary operations. Wormhole and warp proposals require the full geometry and its global causal structure to be examined.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, this is a testable standard for reasoning: identify exactly what the model permits, check its consequences, preserve failures, and keep a mathematically permitted path separate from a physically demonstrated capability.

Sources and further reading

The sources below support the theoretical framework and conditional constructions. They do not establish a BTLB discovery. The numbered calculations in this article are explicit teaching derivations, not numerical results attributed to these papers.

  1. Einstein, A. (1905). “Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper” [On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies]. Annalen der Physik 322(10), 891–921 (also cited as volume 17). DOI: 10.1002/andp.19053221004. English translation. Foundational synchronization and transformation treatment.
  2. Benford, G. A., Book, D. L., and Newcomb, W. A. (1970). “The Tachyonic Antitelephone.” Physical Review D 2, 263–265. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.2.263. Conditional causal difficulties of superluminal signaling.
  3. Morris, M. S., Thorne, K. S., and Yurtsever, U. (1988). “Wormholes, Time Machines, and the Weak Energy Condition.” Physical Review Letters 61, 1446–1449. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.1446. Conditional wormhole time-machine analysis.
  4. Alcubierre, M. (1994). “The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity.” Classical and Quantum Gravity 11, L73–L77. DOI: 10.1088/0264-9381/11/5/001. Author preprint, uploaded in 2000. Speculative metric construction.
  5. Everett, A. E. (1996). “Warp drive and causality.” Physical Review D 53, 7365–7368. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.53.7365. A modified warp construction admitting causal loops.
  6. Hawking, S. W. (1992). “Chronology protection conjecture.” Physical Review D 46, 603–611. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.46.603. Theoretical chronology-protection arguments, not a universal experimental prohibition.

Internal project references

These are supplied project documents, cited by version and section for traceability. They are internal research records, not external peer review. No public URLs are invented.

  • [I1] Beyond the Light Barrier — Research Method v1.2, especially §§2–5, evidence classification, sources, and the mathematics/computation requirements.
  • [I2] Beyond the Light Barrier — Research State v1.11, September 23, 2026; opening current-state statement, §§2–4, 6–8. Retains WC conditional propagation, negative findings, and unresolved WD provenance and feasibility constraints.
  • [I3] Beyond the Light Barrier Shared Field Map v1.0, September 17, 2026; “Comparison queue,” priority 4, and “Claims and maintenance.” A proposed comparison agenda, not proof of completed benchmarks.
  • [I4] BTLB Verification Roadmap v1.1, V5 WD gatekeeping and communication/data-return gate; evidence advancement requirements. Architecture and verification guidance do not establish physical capability.

Publication note: Figure 1 is an AI-generated conceptual scientific illustration, not a numerical simulation, astronomical observation, or physical experiment. No new numerical simulation, independent scientific reproduction, or physical experiment is reported. The arithmetic examples test consequences of explicit hypothetical signaling rules. This Research Explained article is an educational publication milestone, not advancement of a WC or WD model's evidence category.

6. The antitelephone depends on specific assumptions

  
For the simple construction below, assume all of the following:

  

    
- 
      Flat spacetime and the usual Lorentz transformation apply to the stations
      and their clocks.
    

    
- 
      Alice and Bob move inertially relative to each other, and can exchange
      controllable information over hypothetical superluminal links.
    

    
- 
      Each sender can emit toward the other at speed magnitude u > c, forward
      in that sender's own rest-frame time. This availability in both moving
      frames is an extra physical assumption; it is not supplied by the
      coordinate transformation.
    

    
- 
      The required directions, reception, and conditional retransmission are
      possible. In this idealized example Bob replies immediately; real
      processing delays would have to be included.
    

    
- 
      No preferred time ordering or other dynamical restriction forbids one of
      the two links.
    

  

  

    A two-way information channel is crucial. A pattern speed, a correlation
    with no selectable message, or a geometric line on a plot does not provide
    it. A theory that permits superluminal propagation only toward increasing
    time in a preferred frame would not automatically allow this construction.
    Such a restriction would itself need a specified physical theory and tests;
    naming it does not establish viability.
  

  
A complete conditional round trip

  

    Classification: Category 6 — analytic consistency test of hypothetical
      operations.
    This is a separate example from Section 4. Measure positions in
    light-seconds and times in seconds, so c has numerical value 1 in the
    following equations. Let Alice remain at x = 0. Bob passes her at t = 0 and
    moves along x = 0.8t. The primed frame is Bob's rest frame; its origin
    coincides with Alice's at their meeting.
  

  

    Alice waits until event P at (t, x) = (1, 0), then sends at u = 4c in her
    frame. The outgoing path is x = 4(t − 1). It meets Bob where:
  

  

    4(t − 1) = 0.8t,   giving Q: (t, x) = (5/4, 1).
  

  
Transform Q with γ = 5/3:

  

    t′_(Q) = (5/3)(5/4 − 0.8 × 1) = 3/4;   x′_(Q) = 0.
  

  

    Bob immediately sends a reply toward Alice at −4c in his frame. Its path is
    x′ = −4(t′ − 3/4). Alice's worldline in that frame is x′ = −0.8t′. Their
    intersection satisfies:
  

  

    −0.8t′ = −4(t′ − 3/4),   so t′_(R) = 15/16,   x′_(R)
    = −3/4.
  

  
On Alice's worldline t′ = γt, hence:

  

    t_(R) = (15/16)/(5/3) = 9/16 s = 0.5625 s.
  

  

    Alice receives at R, 0.4375 seconds before her transmission at P. Bob's
    reply is forward in his own time: 15/16 − 3/4 = 3/16 second. Alice's
    original transmission is forward in her own time. Yet the combined allowed
    links return information to Alice's earlier proper time.
  

  

    Adding the ordinary future-directed segment of Alice's worldline from R to P
    closes the chain R → P → Q → R. In this toy extension, the two superluminal
    legs are spacelike in the Minkowski metric; the chain is therefore
    not an ordinary general-relativistic closed timelike curve in that
    metric. It is a closed influence loop under the added FTL rules.
  

  

    A self-defeating protocol—“send at P only if no reply arrived at R,” with
    Bob replying whenever he receives—exposes a contradiction if unrestricted
    conditional operations are assumed. This is a consistency problem for that
    set of assumptions, not experimental evidence of messages from the future.
    Restrictions, self-consistency proposals, or other modified dynamics require
    their own analysis; none follows merely from drawing reversed timestamps.
  

  

    Finite delays can remove the loop for a particular setup. Conversely, a
    single unsuccessful arrangement does not prove every possible arrangement
    safe. The allowed speeds, relative motion, separation, response times, and
    channel rules must be analyzed together.
  

  
7. Why wormholes and warp metrics need global analysis

  

    The flat-spacetime calculation cannot simply be pasted onto an arbitrary
    curved spacetime. In general relativity, light cones are defined locally by
    the spacetime metric. A traveler can remain locally slower than light along
    a timelike path, while a hypothetical geometry offers an earlier arrival
    than a specified route through an external region. This is different from a
    local spacelike signal in unchanged Minkowski spacetime.
  

  

    For a proposed traversable wormhole, the complete geometry
    must specify how its two mouths connect, their motion, their clock
    relationship, and the external paths between them. A traversable spatial
    shortcut alone does not establish a time machine. A sufficiently large mouth
    time offset, combined with an available external return path, can create
    closed causal paths in certain models. Morris, Thorne, and Yurtsever
    analyzed this conditional possibility; their paper did not demonstrate a
    constructed wormhole.
    [3]
  

  

    For a proposed warp geometry, local timelike motion does
    not settle the global question either. One must examine the full spacetime,
    including its exterior, transitions, and any allowed combinations of
    journeys. Alcubierre introduced a speculative metric with an effective
    superluminal travel interpretation; Everett subsequently exhibited a
    modified construction admitting causal loops. These are mathematical
    analyses, not propulsion demonstrations, and they do not mean every metric
    described as “warp” has the same causal structure.
    [4]
    [5]
  

  

    A closed timelike curve is a path that remains
    future-directed and timelike locally yet returns to the same spacetime
    event. A closed causal curve can also include null
    segments. These are global geometric properties, independent of coordinate
    relabeling. A proposed FTL channel with additional propagation rules also
    needs analysis of the influence paths allowed by those rules, whether or not
    those paths are metric-causal.
  

  

    One useful sufficient safeguard is a globally defined
    time function that strictly increases along every allowed
    future-directed path. If a path returned to its starting event, the same
    function would have to be both larger and unchanged, which is impossible.
    Finding a coordinate called t is insufficient: its monotonicity must be
    established across the relevant domain and all permitted paths. Failure to
    find such a function is not by itself proof of a loop.
  

  

    Any causal conclusion must state its domain and boundary conditions. A
    finite grid or a single traced ray cannot prove that a loop is absent
    throughout a complete spacetime. Nor does absence of a loop prove that a
    metric has a realizable source, stable evolution, controllable horizons, or
    a feasible creation and shutdown process.
  

  

    Hawking's chronology protection conjecture concerns whether physical laws
    prevent the formation of closed timelike curves. It should not be treated as
    a universal, experimentally established mechanism that automatically repairs
    every speculative geometry.
    [6]

10. What the question really asks us to establish

  

    Two inertial observers can disagree about the order of spacelike separated
    events. They agree on the spacelike classification. A reversal of distant
    coordinate timestamps alone is not a closed causal loop.
  

  

    The serious consistency test begins when a proposed physical mechanism
    supplies controllable connections, return routes, and operational rules.
    Some hypothetical sets of rules produce a reply before the sender's own
    transmission; others restrict the necessary operations. Wormhole and warp
    proposals require the full geometry and its global causal structure to be
    examined.
  

  

    For Beyond the Light Barrier, this is a testable standard for reasoning:
    identify exactly what the model permits, check its consequences, preserve
    failures, and keep a mathematically permitted path separate from a
    physically demonstrated capability.
